h: A fountain fit for a king and a queen waiting on a tower
p: The palace you see began to take shape under James I, who started rebuilding in 1424 after a fire tore through the town. Later kings kept adding to it, and James V, Mary's father, was born here in 1512. He loved the place and lavished money on it, and his most eye-catching addition sits right in the middle of the courtyard: an ornate fountain, carved with figures and decoration, built around 1538. It was carefully restored in the 2000s, and it's one of those details that makes the courtyard feel like a royal stage.

Look up at the north-west corner and you'll see a small room at the top of a tower, known as Queen Margaret's Bower. Legend says Margaret Tudor, wife of James IV, kept watch there in 1513, waiting for news of her husband from the Battle of Flodden. He never came home. It's a poignant spot to think about as you look out over the loch.
Allow around an hour and a half, more if you're walking round the loch as well.

Back in town, the canal basin is home to the Linlithgow Union Canal Society, which runs boat trips along the Union Canal at certain times of year, a lovely gentle way to see the countryside. Look up at St Michael's Church and you'll see its striking modern crown spire, added in the 1960s. Annet House on the High Street is a small museum telling the town's own story. Muiravonside Country Park, a short drive away, is good for a run around with the kids.
